lessons.title: Anchoring Phenomenon & Properties of Similar Figures

quiz.prompt: A school plan is labelled "Scale 1 : 200". A classroom block that is 10 m wide in real life is drawn 5 cm wide on the plan. How many times shorter is a length on the plan than the real length?
quiz.rationale: 10 m = 1000 cm, and 1000 ÷ 5 = 200. Every length on the plan is 200 times shorter than the real length, which matches the label 1 : 200.
quiz.placement: Predict, prompt 1: the classroom block is 10 m wide but appears as 5 cm on the plan

quiz.prompt: A group measures an A4 exercise book (29.7 cm by 21 cm) and an A5 exercise book (21 cm by 14.8 cm). Both length ratios come to about 1.4, and every corner of both books measures 90°. What should the group record?
choices: Not similar: the books have different lengths and widths
Similar: corresponding sides are in the same ratio (about 1.4) and corresponding angles are equal
Not similar: only the angles are equal
Similar: because both books are rectangles, no measuring is needed
quiz.rationale: Both pairs of corresponding sides give a ratio of about 1.4 and all corresponding angles are 90°. Both properties hold, so the books are similar.
quiz.placement: Observe, Task 2 and Task 3: measuring the A4 and A5 exercise books and recording on the Group Observation Chart

quiz.prompt: Two tins have heights of 12 cm and 6 cm. A learner says, "The height ratio is 2, so the tins are similar." What must the group still check before they can say the tins are similar?
choices: That the ratio of the diameters is also 2, and that corresponding angles are equal
Nothing more, because one equal ratio is enough
That the difference in heights equals the difference in diameters
That both tins have the same colour of label
quiz.rationale: Similar figures need all corresponding sides in the same ratio, not just one pair, and equal corresponding angles. The group must check the diameters too.
quiz.placement: Observe, teacher probe: "Have you measured the ratio of heights AND the ratio of diameters?"

quiz.prompt: A small card measures 4 cm by 6 cm. A larger card measures 10 cm by 15 cm. What is the ratio of the corresponding lengths (larger to smaller), found by dividing 10 by 4 and 15 by 6?
quiz.rationale: 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5 and 15 ÷ 6 = 2.5. Both ratios are equal, so the cards are similar, because the corners are all 90° as well.
quiz.placement: Explain, guided example: the 4 cm × 6 cm and 10 cm × 15 cm rectangles

quiz.prompt: Rectangle A is 3 cm by 5 cm and rectangle B is 6 cm by 8 cm. A learner says, "Each side of B is 3 cm longer than the matching side of A, so they are similar." Which statement is correct?
choices: They are not similar, because the angles are different
They are similar, because the differences in length are equal
They are similar, because both are rectangles
They are not similar, because the sides are not in the same ratio (6 ÷ 3 = 2 but 8 ÷ 5 = 1.6)
quiz.rationale: Similarity depends on how many times bigger each side is (the ratio), not on the difference. 6 ÷ 3 = 2 and 8 ÷ 5 = 1.6 are not equal, so the rectangles are not similar even though all their angles are 90°.
quiz.placement: Explain, formative check: catching the additive rather than multiplicative comparison error

quiz.prompt: A 4 cm by 4 cm square and a 4 cm by 8 cm rectangle both have four right angles. Why are they NOT similar?
choices: Their corresponding sides are not in the same ratio (4 ÷ 4 = 1 but 8 ÷ 4 = 2)
Squares can never be similar to anything
The square has a smaller area, and similar shapes must have equal areas
quiz.rationale: Equal angles alone are not enough. Both properties must be true, and here the side ratios are 1 and 2, which are different.
quiz.placement: Explain, formalising PROPERTY 1 (equal corresponding angles) and PROPERTY 2 (corresponding sides in the same ratio) – "these two properties must BOTH be true"

quiz.prompt: Two water tanks on a Kisumu school compound are identical in shape. One holds exactly 8 times as much water as the other, yet it appears only about twice as tall. At the end of this first lesson, which statement is the most honest about what the class knows?
choices: The class already knows the exact rule linking height, area and volume
The tanks are not similar, because their volumes are so different

The class can say the tanks are similar in shape (equal angles, sides in proportion), but how their heights, areas and volumes are related has not yet been explained and stays on the Driving Question Board
The volume must double when the height doubles, so the tank holding 8 times as much must have been measured wrongly
quiz.rationale: Today's lesson establishes what makes shapes similar. The link between lengths, areas and volumes is the Driving Question and will be tested in later lessons, so the predictions stay on the board.
quiz.placement: Driving Question Board: posting the formal Driving Question and pink-note questions about area and volume

lessons.title: Centre of Enlargement and Linear Scale Factor — Finding the Fixed Point

quiz.prompt: A quadrilateral ABCD is enlarged to give a bigger quadrilateral A'B'C'D'. A learner draws straight lines through A and A', B and B', C and C', and D and D', extending each line far in both directions. What will the learner find?
choices: The lines from A and B meet at one point, and the lines from C and D meet at a different point
The four lines all meet at one single point
The four lines go in different directions and never meet
The four lines are parallel to each other
quiz.rationale: In an enlargement, every line through a vertex and its image passes through the same fixed point, the centre of enlargement. Learners who predicted divergence or separate meeting points should revisit the construction.
quiz.placement: Observe: drawing ray lines through A→A', B→B', C→C', D→D' to locate point O

quiz.prompt: A side PQ of a triangle measures 4 cm. In its enlargement, the matching side P'Q' measures 10 cm. What is the linear scale factor (L.S.F)?
quiz.rationale: L.S.F = image length ÷ object length = 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5. Dividing the other way round (4 ÷ 10 = 0.4) is a common reversal.
quiz.placement: Observe: measuring corresponding sides and calculating image ÷ object for each pair

quiz.prompt: O is the centre of enlargement. Point A is 3 cm from O and its image A' is 6 cm from O. A side AB of the object is 4 cm long. How long is the matching side A'B' of the image?
quiz.rationale: L.S.F = OA' ÷ OA = 6 ÷ 3 = 2, and the same scale factor applies to every length. So A'B' = 4 × 2 = 8 cm.
quiz.placement: Observe: measuring OA, OA', OB, OB' and comparing these ratios with the side ratios

quiz.prompt: Which statement best describes the centre of enlargement?
choices: The vertex of the object that is closest to the image
The point where the diagonals of the enlarged image cross
The middle point of the object shape
The single fixed point through which all ray lines joining corresponding vertices of the object and its image pass
quiz.rationale: The centre of enlargement is the one fixed point where all lines through corresponding vertices of the object and image meet. It is not necessarily inside either shape.
quiz.placement: Explain: writing and agreeing on a class definition of 'centre of enlargement'

quiz.prompt: On a school plan, a classroom block that is 10 m wide in real life measures 5 cm. What is the L.S.F from the real building to the plan?
quiz.rationale: Change to the same units: 10 m = 1000 cm. L.S.F = 5 ÷ 1000 = 1/200. It is less than 1 because the plan is smaller than the building.
quiz.placement: Explain: applying L.S.F = image length ÷ object length to the 10 m classroom block on the Kisumu school plan

quiz.prompt: A football pitch is 90 m long. It is drawn on a plan with scale 1 : 200 (L.S.F = 1/200). What length does the pitch have on the plan?
quiz.rationale: 90 m = 9000 cm. Plan length = 9000 × 1/200 = 45 cm. Multiplying by 200 instead gives the wrong, much larger length.
quiz.placement: Explain: practice problem (a), the football pitch on the 1:200 plan

quiz.prompt: A door on a plan with scale 1 : 200 measures 0.45 cm wide. How wide is the real door in metres?
quiz.rationale: Real width = plan width ÷ L.S.F = 0.45 × 200 = 90 cm = 0.9 m. The real door must be bigger than its drawing, so the answer must be more than 0.45 cm.
quiz.placement: Explain: practice problem (b), the door on the plan (homework), used as an end-of-lesson check

lessons.title: Constructing Images under Enlargement on a Plane Surface

quiz.prompt: Point P is 3 cm from the centre of enlargement O. P is enlarged with centre O and linear scale factor (L.S.F) k = 2. Where is the image P'?
choices: 6 cm from O, on the opposite side of O from P
5 cm from O, on the same ray as P
6 cm from O, on the same ray as P (beyond P)
3 cm from O, on the same ray as P
quiz.rationale: For a positive L.S.F the image lies on the same ray from O as the object, at a distance k × OP = 2 × 3 = 6 cm. Adding 2 cm instead of multiplying by 2 is a common error.
quiz.placement: Predict: sketching where image A'B'C' lands for L.S.F = 2 from centre O

quiz.prompt: Point A is 4 cm from the centre of enlargement O. A is enlarged with centre O and L.S.F k = −2. Where is the image A''?
choices: 6 cm from O, on the opposite side of O from A
8 cm from O, on the same side of O as A
2 cm from O, on the opposite side of O from A
8 cm from O, on the opposite side of O from A
quiz.rationale: The distance from O is |k| × OA = 2 × 4 = 8 cm. The negative sign means the image is measured through O to the opposite side.
quiz.placement: Step 3 (k = −2): marking A'' on the opposite side of O

quiz.prompt: A pupil enlarges a triangle with sides 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm using L.S.F = 2. She measures the image sides as 6 cm, 8 cm and 11 cm. Which side shows a construction or measuring error?
choices: The 3 cm side, because 6 ÷ 3 = 2 is too small
The 4 cm side, because 8 ÷ 4 = 2 is too big
No side has an error, because only the total perimeter needs to increase in an enlargement
quiz.rationale: In an enlargement every image side must be exactly k times its object side. The ratios are 2, 2 and 2.2, so the 5 cm side's image should be 10 cm, not 11 cm.
quiz.placement: Step 2: measuring corresponding sides and computing image ÷ object ratios

quiz.prompt: A triangle is enlarged from centre O first with L.S.F = 2 and then with L.S.F = −2. What is the difference between the two images?
choices: The k = −2 image is on the same side of O and in the same orientation, but is twice as small
Both images are the same size, but the k = −2 image is on the opposite side of O and inverted
The k = −2 image is smaller than the k = 2 image
The k = −2 image is on the same side of O as the object but inverted
quiz.rationale: The size of the image depends on |k|, so both images have sides twice as long. The negative sign only places the image on the opposite side of O and inverts it.
quiz.placement: Explain prompt (2): what is different about the image when L.S.F is negative

quiz.prompt: On the school plan, the scale is 1 : 200. A classroom block measures 5 cm on the plan. What is its real length?
quiz.rationale: To go from plan to real building the L.S.F is 200. Real length = 5 × 200 = 1 000 cm = 10 m.
quiz.placement: Explain prompt (3): L.S.F for the 1 : 200 Kisumu school plan and for finding real dimensions

quiz.prompt: Side BC of a triangle is 6 cm long. The triangle is enlarged with a centre O and L.S.F k = −2. What is the length of the image side B''C''?
quiz.rationale: Lengths scale by the size of k: |−2| × 6 = 12 cm. A length cannot be negative, and the negative sign does not make the image smaller.
quiz.placement: Model Building: writing the model statement 'image side = |k| × object side'

quiz.prompt: After constructing enlargements of a triangle with L.S.F k = 2 and k = −2, which statement is firmly established about lengths?
choices: The image sides are in the same ratio to the object sides only when k is positive
Every image side equals k times the matching object side, so a negative k gives a shorter image
Every image side equals |k| times the matching object side; the sign of k only shows which side of O the image lies on
Doubling the lengths of a shape always doubles its area as well
quiz.rationale: The construction and measurements show that the length ratio is |k|, whatever the sign of k. What happens to area and volume has not been investigated yet, and area does not simply double when lengths double.
quiz.placement: Driving Question Board: 'Lengths — SOLVED ✓ | Areas — still to investigate | Volumes — still to investigate'

lessons.title: Enlargement on the Cartesian Plane: Positive and Negative Linear Scale Factors

quiz.prompt: On a Cartesian grid, triangle ABC has vertices A(1, 1), B(3, 1) and C(3, 4). It is enlarged with centre of enlargement the origin O(0, 0) and linear scale factor 2. What are the coordinates of C', the image of C?
quiz.rationale: With the origin as centre, Image = k × Point, so C' = 2 × (3, 4) = (6, 8). Both coordinates double; shifting by 2 or doubling only one coordinate are the common errors.
quiz.placement: Predict: sketching where triangle A'B'C' will appear for the Kisumu School Plan classroom block (centre O, L.S.F. = 2)

quiz.prompt: Point B(3, 1) is enlarged with centre of enlargement the origin O(0, 0) and linear scale factor −2. What are the coordinates of the image B'?
quiz.rationale: Image = −2 × (3, 1) = (−6, −2). Both coordinates are multiplied by −2, so both change sign and double in size.
quiz.placement: Observe: Step 2 — Negative L.S.F. demonstration (L.S.F. = −2 on triangle ABC, centre O)

quiz.prompt: A point is enlarged from a centre of enlargement using a negative linear scale factor. Which statement about its image is correct?
choices: The image is on the opposite side of the centre from the object, at |L.S.F.| times the object's distance from the centre.
The image is on the opposite side of the centre, but at the same distance as the object.
The image is in the same quadrant as the object but smaller.
The image is on the same side of the centre as the object, but further away.
quiz.rationale: A negative L.S.F. places the image on the opposite side of the centre. Its distance from the centre is |L.S.F.| times the object's distance, so the image is turned through 180° about the centre.
quiz.placement: Observe: observation prompt (3) — Where is the image relative to the centre when L.S.F. is negative?

quiz.prompt: Rectangle PQRS has vertices P(1, 2), Q(1, 4), R(3, 4) and S(3, 2). It is enlarged with centre C(1, 2) and linear scale factor 3. What are the coordinates of R', the image of R?
quiz.rationale: Image = Centre + k × (Object − Centre) = (1, 2) + 3 × (2, 2) = (1 + 6, 2 + 6) = (7, 8). Multiplying from the origin would wrongly give (9, 12).
quiz.placement: Explain: Problem 1 (positive L.S.F.) — water tank enclosure P, Q, R, S with centre C(1, 2) and L.S.F. = 3

quiz.prompt: On the school plan, the gate E(2, 1) and F(4, 1) are two corners of triangle EFG. The triangle is enlarged with centre O(0, 0) and linear scale factor −2. What is the length of the image E'F' in grid units?
quiz.rationale: Corresponding lengths are in the ratio |L.S.F.| : 1. EF = 4 − 2 = 2 units, so E'F' = |−2| × 2 = 4 units. A length cannot be negative.
quiz.placement: Explain: Problem 2 (negative L.S.F.) — school gate triangle E, F, G with centre O and L.S.F. = −2, and verifying lengths

quiz.prompt: The Kisumu school plan has scale 1 : 200, and the class lets 1 cm on the plan equal 1 grid unit, so 1 grid unit stands for 2 m on the real compound. The staffroom is at grid point (5, 8) and the gate is the origin. How far is the staffroom from the gate in the x-direction, in metres?
quiz.rationale: 1 grid unit = 2 m, so the x-distance is 5 × 2 = 10 m. The 16 m is the y-distance (8 × 2).
quiz.placement: Model: adding the coordinate grid overlay to the Kisumu School Plan Model (1 grid unit = 2 m)

quiz.prompt: The point (5, 3) is enlarged with centre of enlargement (2, 1) and linear scale factor −2. What are the coordinates of the image?
quiz.rationale: Image = Centre + k × (Object − Centre) = (2, 1) + (−2) × (3, 2) = (2 − 6, 1 − 4) = (−4, −3). Using the origin as centre gives (−10, −6), and using L.S.F. +2 gives (8, 5).
quiz.placement: End of lesson: General Rule — Image = Centre + L.S.F. × (Object − Centre), when the centre is not the origin and L.S.F. is negative

lessons.title: Area Scale Factor: Discovering How Area Grows When You Enlarge a Shape

quiz.prompt: A school plan in Kisumu is drawn at scale 1 : 200, so every length on the plan is 1/200 of the real length. What is the ratio of the real area to the plan area for the same classroom floor?
quiz.rationale: Real lengths are 200 times the plan lengths, so the area ratio is the square of this: 200 × 200 = 40 000. Choosing 200 treats area as scaling in the same way as length.
quiz.placement: Predict: finger-vote on the area ratio for the 1 : 200 classroom plan

quiz.prompt: A rectangle measures 2 cm by 3 cm. It is enlarged with a linear scale factor of 2. What is the area of the enlarged rectangle?
quiz.rationale: Both sides are multiplied by 2, so the image is 4 cm by 6 cm. Its area is 4 × 6 = 24 cm², which is 4 times the object area of 6 cm².
quiz.placement: Observe: drawing and measuring table, row with L.S.F = 2 (2 cm × 3 cm rectangle)

quiz.prompt: A rectangle measures 6 cm by 4 cm. It is reduced to an image with linear scale factor ½. What is the ratio of the area of the image to the area of the object (image ÷ object)?
quiz.rationale: The image is 3 cm by 2 cm, so its area is 6 cm². The object area is 24 cm². The ratio is 6 ÷ 24 = 0.25, which equals (½)².
quiz.placement: Observe: drawing and measuring table, row with L.S.F = ½ (6 cm × 4 cm rectangle)

quiz.prompt: A shop poster is an enlargement of the front face of a 1 kg Unga Pembe packet. The poster has an area 4 times the area of the packet front. What is the linear scale factor from the packet to the poster?
quiz.rationale: A.S.F = (L.S.F)², so L.S.F = √4 = 2. Answering 4 confuses the area scale factor with the linear scale factor.
quiz.placement: Explain: Unga Pembe flour-packet poster problem

quiz.prompt: On a plan drawn at scale 1 : 100, a plot has an area of 12 cm². What is the real area of the plot in m²? (1 m² = 10 000 cm²)
quiz.rationale: The area scale factor is 100² = 10 000, so the real area is 12 × 10 000 = 120 000 cm². Dividing by 10 000 gives 12 m². Multiplying by only 100 gives 1 200 cm², which is 0.12 m² and is wrong.
quiz.placement: Explain: applying A.S.F = (L.S.F)² to the Kisumu school plan and football pitch

quiz.prompt: Which statement correctly completes the class 'What We Now Know' entry about similar figures?
choices: The area scale factor equals the square root of the linear scale factor.
The area scale factor equals the square of the linear scale factor, so doubling lengths quadruples area.
The area scale factor equals the linear scale factor.
If the linear scale factor is 2, the area is also multiplied by 2.
quiz.rationale: The table data showed A.S.F = (L.S.F)²: L.S.F 2 gave 4, L.S.F 3 gave 9, and L.S.F ½ gave ¼. The other statements keep the misconception that area scales like length.
quiz.placement: Driving Question Board: writing the 'What We Now Know' statement

quiz.prompt: On a similarity diagram, a figure has an area of 5 cm². A similar figure is an enlargement of it with linear scale factor 4. What area should be written on the enlarged figure?
quiz.rationale: The area scale factor is 4² = 16, so the new area is 5 × 16 = 80 cm². Multiplying by 4 gives 20 cm², which is the linear-scaling mistake.
quiz.placement: Model Building: adding area labels and the '× (L.S.F)²' arrow to the cumulative similarity diagram

lessons.title: Volume Scale Factor and the LSF–ASF–VSF Relationship

quiz.prompt: A large catering sufuria is geometrically similar to a small home sufuria. Every length on the large one is exactly 2 times the matching length on the small one (diameter 40 cm against 20 cm). How many times as much ugali does the large sufuria hold?
quiz.rationale: LSF = 2, so VSF = 2³ = 8. Doubling every length multiplies volume by 2 × 2 × 2 = 8, not 2 (length) or 4 (area).
quiz.placement: Predict: two sufuria (small and large catering) prediction 'The large sufuria holds __ times as much ugali'

quiz.prompt: Two similar conical grain stores have these dimensions. Small: radius 0.5 m, height 1.2 m. Large: radius 1.5 m, height 3.6 m. What is the Volume Scale Factor (VSF) from the small store to the large store?
quiz.rationale: LSF = 1.5 ÷ 0.5 = 3, so VSF = 3³ = 27. The volumes confirm this: small = ⅓π(0.5)²(1.2) = 0.1π m³ and large = ⅓π(1.5)²(3.6) = 2.7π m³, and 2.7π ÷ 0.1π = 27.
quiz.placement: Observe: Similar Solids Data Card, Pair C (conical grain storage structures)

quiz.prompt: A school has two cube-shaped water tanks. Tank 1 measures 1 m × 1 m × 1 m. Tank 2 is similar and measures 2 m × 2 m × 2 m. Given that 1 m³ holds 1 000 litres, how many litres can Tank 2 hold when full?
quiz.rationale: Volume of Tank 2 = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 m³, and 8 × 1 000 = 8 000 litres. This is 8 times the 1 000 litres in Tank 1, matching VSF = 2³.
quiz.placement: Observe: Similar Solids Data Card, Pair B (cuboid water tanks) and early finishers' calculation of Tank 2 capacity in litres

quiz.prompt: Two similar solids have an Area Scale Factor (ASF) of 36. What is their Volume Scale Factor (VSF)?
quiz.rationale: ASF = (LSF)² = 36, so LSF = 6. Then VSF = 6³ = 216.
quiz.placement: Explain: guided questions Q1–Q3 on the relationship between LSF, ASF and VSF (Scale Factor Law)

quiz.prompt: A small cylindrical water harvesting tank in Kibera holds 500 litres. A geometrically similar large tank has a Length Scale Factor (LSF) of 4. How many litres does the large tank hold?
quiz.rationale: VSF = 4³ = 64, so the capacity is 500 × 64 = 32 000 litres. Using 4² = 16 gives 8 000 litres, which is the area scale factor error.
quiz.placement: Explain: Kibera water harvesting tank problem (LSF = 4, small tank 500 litres)

quiz.prompt: One water tank is exactly twice as tall as a similar tank, yet it holds 8 times as much water. Which statement best explains this?
choices: Doubling the height doubles the volume, so the tank must be wider as well.
The Volume Scale Factor is always 4 times the Length Scale Factor, so 2 × 4 = 8.
Volume depends on three dimensions (length, width, height). Each is multiplied by 2, so the volume is multiplied by 2 × 2 × 2 = 8.
Volume scales in the same way as area, so it is multiplied by 2² = 4 and the remaining factor of 2 comes from the water.
quiz.rationale: For similar solids every dimension is multiplied by k, so volume is multiplied by k × k × k = k³. For k = 2 this gives 8, resolving the water-tank puzzle.
quiz.placement: Driving Question Board: revisiting the Lesson 1 water-tank capacity prediction and writing the 'VSF = (LSF)³' sticky note

quiz.prompt: A cylindrical grain silo in Eldoret is similar to a model silo, and the Length Scale Factor from the model to the real silo is 5. The model holds 12 litres. How many litres does the real silo hold?
quiz.rationale: VSF = 5³ = 125, so the real silo holds 12 × 125 = 1 500 litres. Multiplying by 5 gives 60 litres and multiplying by 5² = 25 gives 300 litres, both of which are wrong.
quiz.placement: Model: extending the Scale Factor Model with the Volume layer, and the Eldoret silo exit task

lessons.title: Application to Real-Life Situations & Model-Building Project Launch

quiz.prompt: A school plan is drawn to Scale 1 : 200. A classroom block measures 4 cm long on the plan. What is the real length of the block?
quiz.rationale: Real length = 4 cm × 200 = 800 cm = 8 m. Learners who divide by 200 get 0.02 cm, and those who forget to convert from cm to m get 800.
quiz.placement: Predict: part (a), real length of the classroom block on the Scale 1 : 200 plan

quiz.prompt: On a plan drawn to Scale 1 : 200, a football pitch measures 25 cm by 15 cm. What is the real area of the pitch?
quiz.rationale: Plan area = 25 × 15 = 375 cm². A.S.F = 200² = 40 000, so real area = 375 × 40 000 = 15 000 000 cm² = 1 500 m². Equivalent check: the real pitch is 50 m by 30 m.
quiz.placement: Predict: part (b), real area of the football pitch from the plan

quiz.prompt: On a Survey of Kenya map drawn to Scale 1 : 50 000, a rectangular rice paddy measures 2 cm by 3 cm. What is the real area of the paddy? (Hint: 1 cm on this map is 500 m in real life.)
quiz.rationale: Map area = 2 × 3 = 6 cm². 1 cm² on this map is 0.25 km², since 1 cm is 0.5 km. Real area = 6 × 0.25 = 1.5 km². Using the linear scale factor on an area, rather than squaring it, gives the wrong answer of 3 km².
quiz.placement: Observe: Card A, Survey of Kenya map (1 : 50 000, Kisumu to Ahero), real area of the rice paddy

quiz.prompt: A square water tank on a plan drawn to Scale 1 : 200 has a 3 cm × 3 cm base and a height of 2 cm on the plan. How many 20-litre jerricans can the full tank fill? (1 m³ = 1 000 litres)
quiz.rationale: Real size is 6 m × 6 m × 4 m, so the volume is 144 m³ = 144 000 litres. Dividing by 20 gives 7 200 jerricans. Equivalently, V.S.F = 200³ = 8 000 000 and 18 cm³ × 8 000 000 = 144 m³.
quiz.placement: Observe: Card B, architectural plan, real volume of the square water tank and number of 20-litre jerricans

quiz.prompt: A mandazi factory in Eldoret enlarges its box design with a length scale factor of 1.5. The original box needs 600 cm² of cardboard. How much cardboard does the new box need?
quiz.rationale: Surface area scales by A.S.F = k² = 1.5² = 2.25, so the new area is 600 × 2.25 = 1 350 cm². Using 1.5 gives 900, and using 1.5³ gives 2 025.
quiz.placement: Observe: Card C, packaging design, mandazi box scaled by L.S.F = 1.5

quiz.prompt: Two water tanks have exactly the same shape. The second tank is twice as tall as the first. How many times as much water does the second tank hold?
quiz.rationale: Volume scales by V.S.F = k³ = 2³ = 8. Doubling the length does not double the volume. Many learners say 2 or 4 because they use k or k².
quiz.placement: Explain: Synthesis Question 1, the two water tanks (2×, 4× or 8×)

quiz.prompt: A scale model of a maize silo has a length scale of 1 : 30. The model's curved surface area is 50 cm². What is the curved surface area of the real silo?
quiz.rationale: Area uses A.S.F = 30² = 900, so real area = 50 × 900 = 45 000 cm² = 4.5 m². Multiplying by 30 gives 0.15 m², and cubing 30 gives 135 m².
quiz.placement: Explain: Synthesis Question 2 (homework), Eldoret maize silo model and real curved surface area

quiz.prompt: A group plans two similar cuboid models using a length scale factor k = 2. Model 1 has a volume of 50 cm³. What is the expected volume of Model 2?
quiz.rationale: Volume scales by V.S.F = k³ = 2³ = 8, so Model 2 has volume 50 × 8 = 400 cm³. Using k gives 100 and using k² gives 200.
quiz.placement: Model: Project Planning Sheet calculation table (L.S.F, A.S.F, V.S.F and expected volume of Model 2)

quiz.prompt: A group builds two similar cylinders. The smaller has radius 3 cm and the larger is made with a length scale factor k = 2. What is the ratio of the curved surface area of the smaller cylinder to that of the larger cylinder?
quiz.rationale: The larger radius is 6 cm. Curved surface area scales by k² = 4, so the ratio is 1 : 4. Using 1 : 2 confuses area with length, and 1 : 8 confuses area with volume.
quiz.placement: Model: group planning check on A.S.F, with the cylinder example (radius 3 cm, k = 2)

lessons.title: Project Presentations, Model Exhibition & Unit Consolidation — Final Explanation

quiz.prompt: A solid is enlarged with a linear scale factor of 2 (every length is doubled). Many learners first predicted that its volume would also double. What is the volume scale factor?
quiz.rationale: Volume scales by k³. With k = 2, the volume scale factor is 2³ = 8, not 2. The answer 4 is the area scale factor.
quiz.placement: Predict: comparing the Lesson 1 prediction with what learners now know about area and volume when scaling by factor 2

quiz.prompt: One group enlarges a small sphere model into a bigger sphere. They find that the volume of the bigger sphere is 27 times the volume of the small one. What linear scale factor did they use?
quiz.rationale: V.S.F = k³ = 27, so k = cube root of 27 = 3. Dividing by 2 or by 3 repeatedly gives the wrong values.
quiz.placement: Observe: group presentations of similar-solid models (stating L.S.F and verifying A.S.F and V.S.F)

quiz.prompt: A Kisumu school plan is drawn to Scale 1 : 200. A classroom 10 m wide appears as 5 cm on the plan. Which statement best explains why only the length is divided by 200?
choices: The scale only works for lengths, so area and volume cannot be compared between the plan and the building.
Areas and volumes are also divided by 200, but the plan only shows lengths.
The scale 1 : 200 compares lengths only. Areas on the plan are 200² times smaller and volumes are 200³ times smaller as a result.
Areas are divided by 200 × 2 and volumes by 200 × 3.
quiz.rationale: A scale such as 1 : 200 is a linear scale factor. Because similar shapes keep their proportions, the area ratio follows as k² and the volume ratio as k³. The scale itself only states the length ratio.
quiz.placement: Explain: Prompt 1 (Why is only the length divided by 200 on the Kisumu school plan?)

quiz.prompt: Two water tanks have exactly the same shape. The larger tank is twice as tall as the smaller one. The smaller tank holds 500 litres. How much water does the larger tank hold?
quiz.rationale: L.S.F = 2, so V.S.F = 2³ = 8. The larger tank holds 500 × 8 = 4 000 litres, so the plumber is correct.
quiz.placement: Explain: Prompt 2 (The plumber says the larger water tank holds 8 times as much water)

quiz.prompt: A building plan is drawn to Scale 1 : 500. What is the ratio of the actual floor area to the floor area on the plan?
quiz.rationale: The L.S.F from plan to building is 500, so the A.S.F = 500² = 250 000. The actual floor area is 250 000 times the plan floor area.
quiz.placement: Explain: Prompt 3 (Nairobi architect, Scale 1 : 500, ratio of actual floor area to plan floor area)

quiz.prompt: A group writes its Final Answer Card about enlarging a solid by a linear scale factor k. Which set of rules should be written on the card?
choices: Lengths scale by k, areas by k², volumes by k³
Lengths scale by k, areas by k, volumes by k
Lengths scale by k, areas by k³, volumes by k²
Lengths scale by k, areas by 2k, volumes by 3k
quiz.rationale: Area has two dimensions, so it scales by k². Volume has three dimensions, so it scales by k³. Scaling all three by k, or by 2k and 3k, are common misconceptions.
quiz.placement: Driving Question Board: writing the group Final Answer Card with the three scale factor rules in symbolic form

quiz.prompt: A learner completes the sentence 'I used to think… Now I know…' about doubling every length of a water tank (k = 2). Which version is mathematically correct?
choices: I used to think the volume would double. Now I know it becomes 8 times bigger, because volume depends on three lengths, so V.S.F = 2³.
I used to think the volume would be 4 times bigger. Now I know it is 2 times bigger, because the radius doubles.
I used to think the volume would be 8 times bigger. Now I know it is only 2 times bigger, because the height is 2 times bigger.
I used to think the volume would double. Now I know it becomes 4 times bigger, because V.S.F = 2².
quiz.rationale: Volume depends on three lengths, so doubling every length multiplies the volume by 2³ = 8. The factor 2² = 4 applies to area, not volume.
quiz.placement: Model Building: individual annotated diagram and 'I used to think / Now I know' reflection
